#9770. A Practitioner's Field Guide to Marketing Engineering

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

My name is Kristina Vislianska. I'm a growth marketer with 10+ years in B2B and B2C SaaS, AI, and Web3, and for the last couple of years, most of what I ship isn't campaigns. It's systems that run campaigns.

At some point, recruiters and founders started calling this "marketing engineering." I had to Google it. Turns out I'd been doing it for a while; I just called it "building stuff so I don't lose my mind doing the same thing every Monday."

This guide is for marketers who want to build, founders who want to hire someone who builds, and engineers who wonder what marketers are doing with their Claude or Codex Pro Max. Everything here comes from systems I built and ran, including the ones that broke.

Marketing engineering turns repeatable go-to-market work into software, combining marketing judgment with engineering skills. Its systems listen to the market, turn what they hear into content, distribute it, and learn from the results. A marketing engineer's output is not a campaign. It's the machine that produces campaigns.

The deliverable is a monitor, a pipeline, an agent or a feedback loop. Something that keeps working when you close your laptop.

And no, it's not "marketing that uses AI tools." Asking ChatGPT for ten hooks is using a tool. Marketing engineering starts when the work keeps running without you typing.

The title keeps changing. A few years ago it was "growth hacker," then "marketing technologist," now "GTM engineer" and "marketing engineer." Honestly, I don't think the title will survive. The skill will.

Marketing ops runs the machine. A GTM engineer builds the machine for sales. A marketing engineer builds the machine for attention. The three roles overlap, and the job titles are still a mess, so here's how I draw the lines.

Marketing ops keeps the existing stack working: clean CRM data, campaign setup, attribution reports. Success looks like data you can trust.

GTM engineers build the revenue engine for sales: enrichment, outbound sequences, lead routing. Success looks like meetings booked and pipeline.

Marketing engineers build the systems that create and distribute marketing: listening tools, content pipelines, community monitors, AI search presence, agents. Success looks like reach, citations in AI answers, and how much one person can run.

Think of a restaurant. Marketing ops keeps the kitchen clean and the orders flowing. The GTM engineer builds the delivery system that gets food to customers who already ordered. The marketing engineer builds the thing that makes people walk past and want to come in. Usually a marketing engineer combines the roles of a whole team of specialists. I like to call them the king of agents and systems.

Everything I've built fits into one of five layers: Listen, Understand, Make, Ship and Learn. I call it the marketing engineering loop, because what you learn at the end changes what you listen for at the start.

Here's the thing most teams get wrong. They start with Make, because "AI writes posts" is the obvious use case. But content volume was never the bottleneck. In my experience the biggest gains sit in Listen and Learn. Listening finds the moments worth acting on. Learning tells you which of your actions actually mattered.

Automate tasks that repeat often and are safe to get wrong. For tasks that repeat often but happen in public, let the machine draft and keep a human on the send button. I call this the frequency × risk matrix.

The most common mistake I see is automating whatever is easiest to automate. That's how you end up with a bot that confidently replies to a grieving customer with a discount code. Two questions work much better: how often does this task repeat, and how bad is it if the machine gets it wrong in front of people? The answer is a split: the machine finds and drafts, a person approves and sends.

Theory is nice, but you came here for the real stuff. Here's one system for each layer of the loop, with what it taught me.

Situation. I wanted to find advisory clients without cold pitching. I hate cold pitching, and so does everyone receiving it. The best moment to talk to a founder is when they post "we just raised" or complain that growth has stalled. Those posts disappear from the feed in hours.

What I built. A radar that searches Threads for pain-point phrases in English and trigger phrases in Ukrainian, like "we raised" or "we got our first revenue." For every match it drafts a reply and pings me in Telegram or email. I read it, rewrite it if needed, and post it myself. The system never posts on its own, and nobody gets a pitch in the first message.

What it taught me. Listening is the cheapest layer to automate and the most valuable. Timing beats copy.

Situation. At an AI workflow automation platform, we were selling agents to small service businesses in seven verticals. To sell to them, we needed to know which tools they already use and what actually makes them swear at their phones.

What I built. A research system that produces three things per vertical: an integration map of the software they already use, a pain-point file built from scraped Reddit threads and classified by an LLM, and ready-made agent templates that solve the top pain with the tools they already have. The research didn't just shape the message. It turned into the product itself: the templates.

What changed. Cost per lead dropped by 80%. Instead of guessing, we shipped 7 agent templates, one per vertical, each built around a pain owners described in their own words. Our one-size-fits-all pitch was gone.

What it taught me. Research is the cheapest way to lower acquisition cost. Before you spend another dollar on ads, find out how your buyers describe their pain. And the same research that shapes your message tells the product team what to build next.

Situation. We needed explainer videos for all seven verticals. We had no video team and no budget to hire one.

What I built. A pipeline where a script goes in and a finished video comes out. The script is split into lines. A voice API generates the voiceover for each line as a separate audio file. Remotion, a React framework for video, renders each scene, and the length of each audio file sets the length of its scene. The on-screen graphics come from a custom skill that holds our whole design system, so every frame follows our brand style guide.

What changed. Seven verticals covered without hiring a single editor. One agent turns a script into a finished, on-brand video in 15 minutes. The pipeline produced 5 videos a day at under $1 each, a fraction of what an agency charges.

What it taught me. When a video costs less than a dollar and 15 minutes, it stops being a project and becomes an experiment. You can test messages in video the way you test headlines. The bottleneck moves from production to knowing what to say, which is exactly why the Listen and Understand layers come first.

Situation. Outreach on X works best when you show up in the right conversation at the right moment. Doing that by hand means scrolling for hours, hoping to catch the one post where someone describes exactly the problem you solve. And by the time you've written a good reply, the moment is gone.

What I built. A browser extension for X that finds outreach opportunities by keywords and trigger phrases, like someone announcing a launch, asking for a tool recommendation or complaining about a problem. When it finds a match, a ready-made prompt system drafts the reply for me in my voice. I read it, tweak it if needed, and send it myself. Every reply gets logged, so the system learns which triggers and formats actually start conversations.

What changed. 20 targeted replies a day, without losing my whole morning. Instead of scrolling for an hour to find two good posts, I review a list of drafts, each tied to a real trigger, and spend my time only on the human part. The logs show which triggers start conversations and which just collect polite likes, so the keyword list gets sharper every week.

What it taught me. Automating Learn isn't about saving time. It's about running enough experiments to see what a platform rewards and punishes. A handful of manual replies will never show you that.

Tools change every few months. These six principles haven't changed across anything I've built, and most of them I learned by breaking something.

You don't need a computer science degree. You climb four rungs: Operator, Assembler, Builder and Architect. Each one needs a different skill, and most marketers get stuck between the second and the third.

Full honesty: I don't write Python from memory. I build with Claude Code and Cursor. What I can do is read the code, understand why it broke, and explain to the AI what to fix. That's the real skill.

The jump from Assembler to Builder isn't about learning to write code. It's about learning to read it well enough to tell why it stopped working at 3 a.m.

Your best first project? Your most boring weekly task. Build the system, put yourself on the send button, and measure what you learn, not the time you save. That's the whole discipline in miniature.

Is marketing engineering the same as growth hacking? No. Growth hacking was about finding clever tactics. Marketing engineering is about building durable systems that run those tactics repeatedly and learn from the results.

Do marketing engineers need to know how to code? They need to read code, not necessarily write it from scratch. With AI coding tools like Claude Code or Cursor, the bottleneck is understanding what broke and why.

What tools do marketing engineers use? Usually LLM APIs, Python or JavaScript, scrapers, no-code automation tools, voice and video AI, etc. The specific tools matter less than the loop they form.

What is the difference between a marketing engineer and a GTM engineer? A GTM engineer builds systems that turn buying signals into sales pipeline. A marketing engineer builds systems that turn market signals into reach, content and visibility.

What should a company automate first in marketing? Tasks that repeat weekly and are safe to get wrong, like monitoring, research and reporting. Public-facing tagive me sks like replies and outreach should be drafted by machines and sent by humans.

Will AI replace marketers? AI replaces repetitive marketing tasks, not marketing judgment. Deciding what to automate, what to say and when a process is broken is still a human job.

Marketing engineering is not about making more content faster. AI already solved that, and honestly, the internet didn't need more of it. It's about building systems that know where to listen, what to say, where to ship it and what to learn from it, while you keep the judgment.

The tools will keep changing. The judgment about what's worth automating is the part that stays yours.

Which layer of the loop have you automated already, and which one do you think is overrated? Tell me in the comments. I read all of them, without a bot.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

#9768. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9767. 5 Common Prescription Drugs Linked To Memory Loss

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Memory loss is not always a result of ageing.

Here are five types of drugs that can affect memory.

The older type of antidepressants — known as tricyclics — have been linked to memory loss.

Around half of people taking them report problems concentrating and one-third say they have memory loss.

Benzodiazepines include drugs marketed under the names Valium, Ativan, Klonopin and Xanax.

These drugs are often prescribed for anxiety and other mental health issues such as OCD, insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unfortunately they are also linked to memory loss and even Alzheimer’s.

Dr Helene Alphonso, a psychiatrist and Director of Osteopathic Medical Education at Texas University, said:

“Current research is extremely clear and physicians need to partner with their patients to move them into therapies, like [modern] anti-depressants, that are proven to be safer and more effective.”

Statins are prescribed to many people to keep their cholesterol in a safer range.

The Food and Drug Administration lists memory loss, forgetfulness and confusion as possible side-effects of the drug.

Some people do report memory problems when taking them, but the studies conducted so far are inconclusive.

Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and are used to lower blood pressure.

They are also prescribed to those with congestive heart problems.

Beta-blockers, though, may also cause the loss of emotional memories.

They have even been tested as a way of treating post-traumatic stress disorder because of their ability to block emotional memories.

Again, though, the studies are not conclusive.

People who cannot sleep are sometimes prescribed so-called ‘Z-drugs’.

The ‘Z-drugs’ have been linked to memory loss: especially losing the ability to make new memories.

They have also been reported to cause strange behaviours like driving or cooking with absolutely no memory of the event.

Where possible consider a psychological therapy or applicable alternative to using these drugs.

Naturally, you should always consult your physician before making changes to your medication.

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9766. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

#9765. Debugging Missing Results in a Multistage Search Pipeline

Senior software engineer building search, ranking, personalization, and ML infrastructure. I write about AI evaluation and distributed systems

Senior software engineer building search, ranking, personalization, and ML infrastructure. I write about AI evaluation and distributed systems

Senior software engineer building search, ranking, personalization, and ML infrastructure. I write about AI evaluation and distributed systems

A reader searches a library catalog for a book the library definitely owns. The request succeeds, latency looks normal, and the results page is full of plausible alternatives. The expected book is missing.

The ranking model is the obvious suspect. But tweaking scores cannot help if the book never reaches the model. It might be absent from the serving index. Retrieval might cut it off at a candidate limit. A filter might reject it on a technicality. Or the page might lose it during assembly. Each explanation needs different evidence and a different fix.

The argument of this piece: before you tune anything, find the first stage where your candidate stopped progressing. Everything else follows from that.

A good score in a report can be misleading here. A book that would have ranked first still cannot appear if it was never in the ranking input. Counterfactual scores do not describe the actual request.

Most search systems pass candidates through the same five stages. A missing result means the candidate left this chain at some point, or never entered it.

Walk these in flow order. Later stages inherit everything earlier stages did wrong. The first link that broke is the one to fix.

“Search quality got worse” is too broad to debug. You need one specific request and one specific item: item b04 was missing from request R, which used index snapshot S and configuration C. That gives you something to reproduce.

Preserve the context: normalized query, locale, eligibility rules, experiment assignment, and personalization inputs. A replay against today's index with default settings may describe a different request. Keep sensitive inputs under access control.

Request timings tell you where a system spent time, not where the result set changed. For diagnosis, you want each stage's decision on a candidate: kept, dropped, or never seen, plus the reason.

A compact event record works well: request ID, candidate ID, stage, action, and a reason code. Ranking events can add score and position; display events can note items cut by the page limit. Keep shared context such as index, model, and code versions in a request-level record so you do not repeat it per event.

Two cautions. First, a reason code records what the code decided, not that the decision was right. An event saying language mismatch only helps if you check the stored value, the requested value, and the intended comparison rule. Otherwise it just labels a wrong decision.

Second, some candidates have no events at all. If retrieval never emitted the item, there is nothing to record downstream, and the absence of events cannot distinguish an indexing failure from a cutoff or a query mismatch. Keep two extra facts for those cases: does the item exist in the request's snapshot, and where does it sit in the full retrieval ordering? A position beyond the candidate limit explains the silence. In production, use a targeted lookup against the same snapshot or a controlled replay, and write down what the diagnostic actually proved. Say unknown where the evidence runs out.

Consider a fictional library catalog where our target book is fourth in retrieval order but would rank first on relevance if it reached the ranker. Three separate faults remove it, each at a different stage.

The first fault is a stale index snapshot: the current catalog has the book, but the snapshot the request served from omits it. A membership check against that snapshot comes back false, stopping the investigation before retrieval or ranking. That establishes absence from that snapshot, nothing more. Ingestion failures, rejected documents, or a request routed to an older generation could each be upstream causes, so you need ingestion and routing evidence to tell them apart. Verify fixes against the snapshot the request actually used.

The second fault is a filter rejecting an eligible item. The book reaches retrieval with stored language en, but a bad configuration requests EN and compares with case-sensitive equality, so the filter event reports a language mismatch. Comparing the stored value against the intended lowercase contract exposes the mistake. The telltale symptom is breadth: this fault rejects every retrieved book, so the displayed set is empty. The fix follows the field's contract. Do not normalize blindly, though; some identifiers are case-sensitive by design, and authorization rules deserve stronger guarantees than a convenient string conversion.

The third fault is retrieval truncating the candidate set. The book is in the snapshot and fourth in retrieval order, but the configuration retrieves only three candidates. The filter never receives it, so there is no filter event at all. Membership lookup, retrieval position, and the configured limit together locate the loss. In production, raising candidate counts adds retrieval, feature-loading, and ranking cost, so measure cost and coverage before making it the general answer.

When candidate IDs are stable, a baseline run and the changed run are easy to compare. Walk both histories in pipeline order and stop at the first divergence. If the snapshots differ, a later score difference is probably a consequence of changed inputs, not a model problem. If retrieval is identical but filtering differs, compare filter inputs and rules before you retrain anything.

Also mark your evidence complete or truncated. A request that timed out halfway should not look like a complete history.

Recording every candidate transition for every request grows with traffic and candidate counts. Sample bounded diagnostics, cap the event budget, and keep retention short. Keep lightweight stage counts everywhere, and collect detailed histories only for selected investigations.

When one of those lacks evidence, report the gap. The next useful change may be better instrumentation, not a different ranking model.

Most missing-result investigations end where they should have started: the stage that quietly dropped the candidate. Ask where it stopped progressing, collect evidence at that boundary, and the fix usually becomes obvious.

Senior software engineer building search, ranking, personalization, and ML infrastructure. I write about AI evaluation and distributed systems

#9762. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9761. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.

  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.

  • Free mobile apps

Grammarly Cons

  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey

ProwritingAid Pros

  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.

ProWritingAid Cons

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.

  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9760. 'Almost Right' Agent Code Is Worse Than Wrong Code. It's Devs' Top AI Complaint

Posted on Nov 8 • Edited on Nov 8 • AI-assisted

A support ticket says some orders never show up in a customer's order history, and only for some customers. Someone who never saw the change opens the pagination helper and finds Math.floor where Math.ceil belongs. Proving it takes the afternoon.

Three weeks earlier, an agent wrote that helper. The tests were green and the 40-line diff read the way you would have written it, so you approved it before your coffee cooled.

That bug was never wrong enough to get caught.

In Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey, 66% of the 31,476 developers who answered the question on frustrations with AI tools picked "AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite." It was the most common answer. Second, at 45.2%, was "Debugging AI-generated code is more time-consuming."

Here is my take: almost-right agent code is worse than wrong code. Wrong code costs you a retry. Almost-right code costs you a bug in production, found later by someone with less context than you had at review time.

The same 2025 survey page shows the trust problem behind that frustration. More developers distrust the accuracy of AI tools (46%) than trust it (33%). Only 3.1% highly trust it. And 84% use AI tools or plan to, up from 76% the year before.

Most developers use these tools, and 51% of professional developers use them daily. Many of them doubt what comes out. That is a workable position, as long as the doubt turns into checking. It usually turns into reading.

Stack Overflow's 2026 AI results don't repeat the frustrations question, so 2025 is the latest reading on "almost right." The 2026 page does have this: 48% of respondents say they trust AI "when they can easily validate the answers." Reading a diff is not validating it.

Wrong code fails loudly. It doesn't compile or a test goes red. Sometimes the agent itself says it couldn't finish. You throw it away and try again, and the cost is a few minutes and some tokens.

Almost-right code compiles. It passes the happy-path test and looks like code your team writes. So it passes the review it gets, which on a busy afternoon is a skim. Then it lands.

The bill comes later, and it's bigger. The person debugging it doesn't have the prompt or the turn where the mistake went in. They have a symptom and a git blame pointing at a function that looks fine.

There is data that AI-written PRs carry more logic errors. CodeRabbit's December 2025 report looked at 470 open-source pull requests (320 AI-co-authored, 150 human-only) and found about 1.7× more issues in the AI ones, with logic and correctness issues 75% more common. Two caveats: CodeRabbit sells AI code review, and the authors say they "cannot guarantee all the PRs we labelled as human authored were actually authored only by humans."

The obviously broken part never ships. The one that is almost right does.

The bug from the opening fits in a few lines:

It looks right. With 100 orders and 20 per page it returns 5, which is correct. A test for the case the agent had in mind passes too. Here it is, written for Node's built-in test runner:

That test passes against the wrong code. Add one order and the answer should be 6. Math.floor(101 / 20) is 5, so the 101st order never gets a page. One more test catches it before anyone ships it:

The fix is Math.ceil. The point is that no amount of staring at the first version would have made you more confident than that one red test.

An agent works in turns. It reads files, edits, runs something, edits again. You usually see the result once, as one diff at the end, with every turn squashed together.

In a 600-line diff where 590 lines are fine, the 10 bad ones sit between good ones. The good lines buy trust you then spend on the bad ones. The longer the diff, the more your review turns into a skim, and the skim is exactly the review almost-right code passes.

One long diff gets a skim. Short pieces, each with a check that runs, get a verdict.

Two habits change that. Check each piece of work while it's small, ideally per turn. And make "done" something a machine runs instead of something you feel after reading.

Start with a script any agent can be told to run, and that you run before you accept the work:

set -e stops at the first failing command, so a red type check never hides behind a green test run. Drop the tsc line if the repo isn't TypeScript, and make sure npm test runs something, for example "test": "node --test" in package.json.

Then wire it into the agent so it can't report "done" without it. In Claude Code, a Stop hook fires when Claude finishes responding, and exit code 2 from that hook "sends Claude back to keep working." For other agents, check their docs for a way to run a command when a turn ends, or run the script yourself before you accept anything.

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this part with that in mind. In Hermes, your own checks can decide when a task is done, and Land then commits, opens a pull request or merges locally in one step, with undo (README).

The other half is reviewing in small pieces. Hermes saves every agent turn, so you can diff or restore a single turn, with undo. The Review Desk (⌘G, or Ctrl+Shift+G on Windows and Linux) shows those changes by turn or by file.

The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view: two turns (T1: 3 files +69 −1, T2: 1 file +1 −0), turn 1's diff of src/db.ts adding a refunded status, the changed files, and a commit message drafted from the turns.

In that view, T2's single line gets read on its own. Squashed into one diff with T1's 69, it would be the kind of line where a floor slips past.

Checks only catch what someone thought to check. The paging test exists because someone thought of 101 orders. If the agent writes the tests for its own code, they can carry the same misunderstanding as the code. So read the tests before you read the implementation, and write the edge case yourself when it matters.

Hermes doesn't judge whether code is correct either. It shows you each turn and leaves the decision to you. It never answers a permission prompt for you and never types into a terminal on its own.

Start with the cheapest version: write the 101-orders test for whatever paging helper your agent last touched.

What's your "almost right" story? Was it caught in review, by a test, or by a customer? Tell me in the comments.

A done-check is the smallest eval there is: a command that says whether the output is right. When an LLM feature runs in production, the same question turns into traces and evals, and the LLM Observability Pocket Guide is my short guide to picking the tools for that. If you want to review agent work turn by turn on your own repo, Hermes IDE is a free download for macOS, Windows and Linux, source-available under BSL 1.1 on GitHub, and not affiliated with Nous Research, Anthropic, OpenAI or any other agent vendor.

#9759. SSH host key fingerprints and configurations

The first time you SSH into a fresh server, your terminal stops and asks you a question:

The authenticity of host '203.0.113.10' can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:9mYvLzQ... Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?

Most people type yes and move on. I used to do the same. Then I stopped to think about what that yes actually means.

That fingerprint is a hash of the server's host key. It is the one thing proving the machine on the other end is the machine you think it is. The IP address proves nothing — IPs get reassigned, DNS gets pointed at the wrong place, and a network in between can answer for a host that isn't there. The fingerprint is the identity. Typing yes without checking it is trusting a stranger because they answered the door.

So my rule is simple: I check the fingerprint once, from a place I trust, before I ever type yes.

The easiest source is the provider. When I spin up a server, the cloud console shows the host key fingerprint for that instance. I copy it, compare it character for character with what the terminal shows, and only then type yes. If they don't match, I stop. No retry, no "probably fine", no clearing known_hosts and trying again. A mismatch is the whole warning system working as designed, and the correct response is to find out why before connecting.

If the console doesn't show it, I get the fingerprint a different way: ssh-keyscan from a network I already trust, or ssh-keygen -l against the public key file on the server through a channel I already verified. The point is the same — the fingerprint comes from somewhere other than the connection I'm about to trust. Checking the fingerprint against the same untrusted connection proves nothing.

Once I've verified it, SSH remembers it for me. The fingerprint goes into ~/.ssh/known_hosts on first connect, and from then on every connection is checked silently. That is the part people forget: the first yes is the only one that matters. Every connection after it is just confirming nothing changed.

And when it does change, SSH will tell you loudly — a big warning about a possible man-in-the-middle, connection refused. Most people's instinct is to delete the old line and reconnect. Sometimes that's right: I rebuilt the server, the host keys were regenerated, the fingerprint legitimately changed. But "sometimes" is doing a lot of work there. When I see that warning, I verify first. Did I actually rebuild this machine? Did the provider rotate the key? If I can't answer yes to something concrete, I don't connect until I can.

When the change is legitimate, I update the record deliberately: ssh-keygen -R hostname removes the old entry, then I verify the new fingerprint the same way I did the first time and connect. Deliberately, not by deleting the whole known_hosts file because it was faster.

The other half of this piece is the config file, and it's the boring half that saves the most mistakes. I don't type IP addresses, ports, and key paths from memory. They live in ~/.ssh/config:

Host api HostName 203.0.113.10 User ubuntu Port 2222 IdentityFile ~/.ssh/api_ed25519

Now ssh api is the whole command. The port can't be forgotten, the wrong key can't be offered, the username can't be mistyped. Each host gets its own block, each key its own file, and the config is the one place where all of it is written down. A new machine, a fresh checkout of my dotfiles, and I can reach every server I manage without reconstructing anything from memory.

Two settings I leave alone: StrictHostKeyChecking stays on. The accept-new middle ground looks convenient, but it turns the first connection back into an unchecked yes, which is the exact thing the fingerprint is there to prevent. And I never share one key across everything — one key per purpose, so revoking one doesn't mean re-keying the world.

None of this is advanced. It's a fingerprint check and a config file. But the fingerprint is the only moment SSH asks you to actually verify the identity of the machine you're about to hand your credentials to, and the config file is what stops the small mistakes that lead to the big ones. I check once, properly, and then I let the tooling do the watching.

#9758. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9755. Alt-Svc moves HTTP authority to a second endpoint

An Alt-Svc response tells a client that another endpoint can serve the same origin. The mechanism is common in HTTP/3 deployments, where a website advertises a QUIC service on another port. It also changes where requests travel. That makes the header, the advertised endpoint, and the client's fallback behavior part of the security boundary.

RFC 7838 says an alternative service is authoritative for the origin. When a client uses one, it presents the origin's SNI and Host information to that service. The alternative is expected to establish the same security properties as the origin. A header injected into a user-controlled response, an endpoint that accepts a different certificate, or an unsafe fallback can therefore turn a performance feature into traffic redirection or downgrade.

Proxies and gateways often inspect the origin hostname while treating the advertised port as infrastructure detail. A policy that allows the origin on TCP 443 may not describe how the same origin behaves when it is reached through a QUIC listener on another port. Firewall rules, certificate inventories, observability, and request authentication should follow the effective host and service.

The RFC's security section warns that an attacker able to inject alternative services and listen at the advertised port can impersonate the origin. The risk is reduced by requirements on how alternatives are associated with an origin, but deployment mistakes can undermine those expectations. The client must negotiate the expected protocol and must regard Alt-Svc as part of the origin's authority, not as permission to route to an arbitrary host.

Connection coalescing adds another question. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 can reuse a connection for multiple origins when the certificate and authority conditions allow it. RFC 8336 defines an ORIGIN frame that lets a server add origins to a connection's origin set. A reverse proxy should know which origins it groups and should not assume that a single upstream connection represents a single tenant.

Inventory Alt-Svc generation at the CDN, reverse proxy, and application layers. Determine which components can set the header and whether user content can influence response headers. Strip backend-generated Alt-Svc headers at an edge that is not prepared to support the advertised service. Restrict who can open the advertised listener.

Check proxy and TLS-inspection behavior. A client configured to use a proxy should route the alternative service through that proxy unless the configuration explicitly allows a direct connection. An inspection appliance that sees HTTP/2 but not QUIC can create a blind spot. The control should be an explicit choice about whether QUIC bypasses inspection, not an accidental consequence of a browser update.

Review cache lifetime and deletion behavior. An old advertisement can outlive a migration. Remove stale ports and ensure that decommissioned endpoints no longer receive authoritative requests. Monitor clients that still use retired alternatives.

From an external network, request the origin and inspect the returned Alt-Svc value. Resolve the endpoint through the same DNS and proxy path a client uses. Check the certificate, ALPN, Host header handling, HTTP/3 support, and fallback behavior. Send requests for a second origin to see whether connection reuse crosses a tenant or service boundary.

Test responses to a modified or malformed advertisement. The client should reject an invalid value rather than fall back to an unauthenticated endpoint. Test an endpoint that stops answering. The fallback plan should preserve the origin's required security properties and should be observable.

Treat Alt-Svc as an authority delegation record. Generate it only from trusted configuration, publish only endpoints with matching certificate and routing policy, and keep every such endpoint in the asset inventory. Inspect the same traffic path that clients actually use. When QUIC cannot be inspected or controlled as well as the origin, do not advertise it merely because the server supports it.

The goal is not to avoid HTTP/3. It is to make the alternate endpoint carry the same identity, access, and observability rules as the origin it claims to serve.

#9754. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain.
