#9734. Your Prospecting Play Changed. Enrolled Contacts May Still Be Running the Old One.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero image: Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

A sales team fixes a weak claim in its prospecting instructions and assumes the campaign is corrected. Tomorrow, a previously enrolled contact receives outreach generated under the earlier configuration. The change was real. The assumption about its scope was wrong.

That is a release-management problem, not merely a copywriting problem. HubSpot's Prospecting Agent combines targeting, research, drafting, enrollment, and execution. Each step needs a separate state if the team wants to explain what happened to a particular prospect.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

I would model a prospecting play as a versioned deployment with a queue, not as a prompt that everyone assumes is always current. That model makes a documented product behavior visible: editing a play does not automatically update every contact already running through it.

HubSpot's Prospecting Agent guide states that play edits apply to newly enrolled contacts; existing contacts continue with the version published at enrollment. It also documents review-before-send and send-without-review modes, sender fallbacks, outreach guardrails, and the inability to perform credit-consuming agent actions in sandbox accounts.

Those details are enough to change the deployment design. A play update is not a global patch. It creates at least two populations: new enrollments using the revised play and earlier enrollments retaining the previous version. The team needs to know which population requires intervention.

The architecture below is proposed. Example fields, states, and calculations are not native HubSpot property names or a promise that the agent exposes every detail through an API. Implement only what your actual account and supported interfaces can verify.

A company can exhibit a buying signal without being eligible for outreach. A contact can match a persona without being the appropriate person for this message. A recommendation can be useful without being ready for execution.

Use separate gates for fit, signal relevance, contact identity, relationship state, outreach eligibility, and owner assignment. Do not collapse them into a single agent-ready score.

In a hypothetical example, an account announces a new funding round. That signal may justify research. It does not establish a particular employee's responsibility, prove interest in your offer, or authorize an email. The next step should be an evidence-backed review of the account and intended recipient, not an automatic leap from company event to personal claim.

Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

A useful integration-owned queue could distinguish candidate, researched, eligibility-reviewed, draft-ready, approved, scheduled, sent-confirmed, response-received, and stopped. A contact should not move to sent-confirmed because a draft exists or because enrollment succeeded.

For each transition, record the evidence that supports it. A scheduled state needs a schedule reference. A sent-confirmed state needs evidence from the owning delivery system. A response-received state needs an actual inbound response, not an open event or a task marked complete.

The queue should also retain why an item stopped. Missing evidence, a relationship conflict, an outdated play, and a disconnected sender are different operational problems. They need different owners and recovery steps.

Avoid overwriting all of them with a generic failed status. That makes retrying look easy while hiding the business reason the action should not proceed. A successful recovery may mean intentionally not sending anything.

At enrollment, preserve the contact identifier, company association, play reference, known play revision or captured configuration, eligibility decision, intended sender policy, and time of enrollment. Record the limit of what you can actually observe.

The configuration label is an example organizational reference, not an invented HubSpot version identifier. If the native interface shows only a play name, retain an approved configuration snapshot and document that limitation.

This receipt enables a bounded question during a correction: which contacts entered under the configuration affected by this issue? Without it, teams may either miss affected contacts or stop unrelated work unnecessarily.

When a play changes, classify the change. A harmless style adjustment is different from a withdrawn offer, corrected product claim, new suppression rule, or sender-ownership correction.

For consequential changes, identify the earlier enrollment cohort and decide what to do with its pending work. The answer may involve pausing, reviewing, unenrolling, or rebuilding drafts through supported product controls. Do not assume a save operation performs those steps automatically.

Maintain a migration plan before editing an active play. It should specify the affected cohort, action owner, treatment of pending messages, treatment of already sent messages, and verification evidence. Never describe a configuration rollback as recall of an email that already reached a recipient.

A message correction may also require direct human communication. That is a separate external action with its own approval, not an automatic consequence of editing a play. The technical workflow should preserve that distinction.

Sender identity affects relationship ownership, reply routing, and the meaning of the message. A fallback sender can prevent a process from stopping, but it can also create an interaction the intended account owner did not expect.

Test a connected owner inbox, a missing owner, a disconnected inbox, and an owner change after enrollment. Specify whether a fallback is acceptable for each play. If it is not, use a hold and an owner queue instead of silently selecting another identity.

The product documents sender options and fallbacks. Your deployment should determine what they mean operationally. A technical ability to send on behalf of a user is not a blanket authorization for every message or every commercial relationship.

Define the organization's approval policy before rollout and keep drafts unsent until the applicable gate is satisfied. Describing an autonomous capability is not the same as authorizing its use in a live account. Review scope should include the actual recipient, sender, subject, body, links, and attachments, not merely the play's general purpose.

Natural-language instructions are useful for tone and content. Use explicit product controls for the frequency and timing constraints the interface supports. Do not rely on a sentence in the prompt to enforce a critical cap.

Test the combination of business days, send windows, fallback time zone, and the actual contact time-zone data you have. A missing or incorrect time zone is a data-quality issue. A polished preview does not prove when the recipient will receive the message.

Also inspect overlapping outreach systems. A contact may be eligible for more than one play, sequence, or manual campaign. Define a cross-channel ownership policy so that local limits do not produce excessive aggregate activity.

That policy may require coordination outside the agent. State the limitation openly. Do not claim a native account-wide deduplication or suppression guarantee unless it has been verified for the exact configuration and channels involved.

A relevant signal can support a reason to research without supporting the exact wording of an email. A hiring announcement does not necessarily prove a technology migration. An old CRM note does not necessarily support a current product promise.

Require each consequential factual claim in a draft to have a current, suitable source. Remove claims that exceed the evidence. Prefer a modest question grounded in verified context over a confident explanation of a prospect's internal priorities.

The NIST Generative AI Profile discusses content provenance and assessment limitations. Here, I would apply that principle to a claim review record that identifies the source, date, supported statement, and uncertainty. That is a proposed practice, not a native agent audit feature.

HubSpot's AI-settings documentation also distinguishes data-source access from model-training controls. Neither configuration decision replaces review of an outbound message's recipient, claims, or audience suitability.

The sandbox limitation for credit-consuming Prospecting Agent actions matters. Do not label a mock demonstration an end-to-end delivery test. Split verification into layers: synthetic policy tests, configuration inspection, draft review, and a separately authorized controlled execution test if needed.

Use fictional contacts and signals for deterministic checks. Test duplicate candidate intake, withdrawn offers, changed ownership, missing time zones, old play enrollment, unsupported claims, and an ineligible contact entering through a different trigger.

For every fixture, document the expected stop or continuation. Record which layers were tested and which remain unverified. A review-only pilot is useful even when it does not prove autonomous delivery. It can reveal the quality and exception workload before broader exposure.

Never send a test email simply because it is called a test. The recipient, content, account, and approval policy still matter. A production test is an external communication, not a harmless extension of research.

Track candidates, eligible contacts, drafts reviewed, approved drafts, verified sends, actual replies, qualified conversations, and opportunity outcomes separately. Add rejection reasons and review effort. That gives the team a way to distinguish targeting problems from content problems or delivery problems.

A hypothetical increase in generated drafts is not proof of improved pipeline. A higher approval rate can mean better drafts, weaker review, or a change in the audience. Keep the denominator and cohort definition attached to every metric.

Use Agent Hub's documented workspace for the outcomes it actually exposes, then reconcile additional measures from their owning systems. Do not infer business results from a green completion indicator.

The useful technical question is not whether the agent can produce outreach. It is whether the team can explain which play, evidence, eligibility decision, sender, approval, and delivery receipt produced one particular message. That explanation is what makes a prospecting system governable when the play changes.

Documentation checked October 20, 2026. No live agent, enrollment, message, or account setting was changed for this article.

For the message-level evidence boundary, see a claim-validation workflow for AI-generated customer emails. The framework above applies that boundary to this specific feature and its failure modes.

Before Moving Contracts Into Revenue Hub, Prove Who Will Send the Next Invoice.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

#9733. ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

#9732. Wholesale prices for tagged customers on Shopify, without a second store

A lot of small Shopify stores end up with a few wholesale buyers almost by accident: a café that wants your coffee by the case, a boutique that resells your candles, a gym that orders shakers in bulk. They shouldn't pay retail, but setting up a whole B2B operation for five accounts feels like overkill.

This post walks through the usual options, what each one is good and bad at, and a simple setup based on customer tags. I'm writing it as AppVerix, a small studio that makes Shopify apps (one of them does this, mentioned at the end), but the first part applies whatever you end up using.

1. A separate wholesale store. Clean separation, but you now maintain two catalogs, two inventories (or a sync app), two themes and usually two subscriptions. For a handful of buyers, that's a lot of upkeep.

2. Manual draft orders or invoices. The buyer emails you a list, you build a draft order with a custom discount and send an invoice. It works and costs nothing, but every order goes through you, and mistakes (wrong price, wrong quantity) are easy.

3. Discount codes for wholesale buyers. You create a code and limit who can use it to specific customers or a customer segment. Better than invoices, but buyers have to remember to type the code, codes can leak, and a plain discount code doesn't stop someone from placing a two-unit "wholesale" order.

4. Shopify's built-in B2B features (companies, catalogs, payment terms). This is the full system: company accounts, locations, price lists per catalog, net terms. It's powerful, but it's also a real setup project, and which parts you get depends on your Shopify plan. Check your own admin and plan before you count on it.

For many stores the gap is in the middle: you want buyers to log in and just see their price, with a few sensible rules, without modeling companies and catalogs.

Customer tags are already in every Shopify plan, so they make a good foundation.

Step 1: tag your wholesale customers. In the customer's page, add a tag such as wholesale. If you have tiers, use separate tags (wholesale, distributor). Keep the names boring and consistent; you'll be filtering by them later.

Step 2: decide the discount per group, not per product. A single percent off per group ("wholesale gets 30% off") is much easier to maintain than a price for every variant. Then add exceptions only where margins need them, for example 15% on a low-margin collection, or 0% on gift cards.

Step 3: set minimums that match how you actually ship. This is the part people skip, and it's where wholesale loses money. Common rules:

Write these down before you configure anything. If a buyer asks "why can't I check out?", you want a clear answer.

Step 4: make reordering fast. Wholesale buyers reorder the same things. A table where they can type quantities across a whole collection, or paste a list of SKUs and quantities, saves them far more time than any discount.

Step 5: tell them they're logged in. A small banner like "Wholesale prices applied" stops a lot of support emails from buyers who forgot to sign in and are seeing retail prices.

Full disclosure: we make AppVerix Wholesale, which does the setup above. You create a group for a customer tag with a percent off, add optional percents for specific products or collections (0 leaves a product out), and set order minimums: amount, units, units per product and case-pack multiples. Signed-in tagged customers get the discount in the cart and at checkout. It also adds a quick order form block (collection table, SKU search, paste "SKU,qty" lists) and a banner to your theme.

What it isn't: it's not a company-account or catalog system, and it doesn't set fixed prices per variant. If you need net terms, company locations or per-catalog price lists, Shopify's B2B features are the better fit. Plans start at $19/month with a 7-day free trial (current pricing is on the listing).

Whatever you use, the order is the same: tag the buyers, keep one discount per group, set minimums that match your packaging, and make reordering painless. Questions about a specific setup are welcome in the comments.

#9731. Arc Browser in 2026: Worth Leaving Chrome For?

Posted on Nov 8 • Originally published at pikvue.com

Arc Browser has been called the Chrome replacement we've been waiting for. Its workspace-and-spaces model is the most significant rethink of browser UI in years. But innovation doesn't automatically mean better. Here is where the approach holds up, where it gets in the way, and who should actually switch.

Arc Browser (2026) is the most innovative desktop browser available today — if you're on a Mac. Its Spaces-based tab management, auto-archive, and split-view completely rethink how we organize our browsing life. The learning curve is real, and the Windows version is still catching up, but for knowledge workers drowning in tabs, Arc is a revelation.

Overall Rating: 8/10 Target audience: Mac-based power users, project jugglers, and tab hoarders.

Arc reimagines the browser interface from the ground up. Instead of a traditional tab bar across the top, Arc uses a persistent sidebar with Spaces (grouped workspaces), pinned tabs, and easels (visual boards). It's built on Chromium, so all Chrome extensions work, but it feels nothing like Chrome. The command palette (⌘+T) acts as a universal search bar, letting you navigate tabs, bookmarks, history, and even perform browser actions without touching the mouse. The concept is simple: your browser should adapt to how you think, not the other way around.

The verdict on Arc's space management is clear from how the product is built: it is genuinely transformative for anyone who lives in a browser. Switching between a "Work" Space (pinned Gmail, Slack, Notion) and a "Personal" Space (Reddit, YouTube, shopping) takes a single keystroke, and the muscle memory forms fast because Spaces map onto how you already separate contexts. Auto-archive is the feature that changes daily behaviour — old tabs leave the bar silently but stay searchable, so the bar stops being an archaeological record of the last three weeks.

However, the weaknesses are real. The lack of a mature extension ecosystem beyond Chrome Web Store means you won't find Arc-exclusive tools. Occasional rendering issues on complex sites (notably Google Docs and Figma) forced me back to Chrome for those specific tasks. And the Windows version, while functional, clearly lags behind the macOS experience — animations are less smooth, and some features (like Little Arc and Boosts) feel incomplete.

Arc is the most innovative browser since Chrome launched in 2008. Its Spaces + auto-archive tab management genuinely changed how I browse and work. It's not for everyone — the sidebar paradigm and Mac-first limitation are real tradeoffs — but for its target audience (Mac-based knowledge workers and tab hoarders), it's the best browser available today.

That said, Arc is best as a personal browsing browser. Keep Chrome or Brave for development work, heavy extension use, and cross-platform consistency. One browser to live in, another to work in — that's the pragmatic 2026 setup.

Overall Rating: 8/10 — Best-in-class tab management, Mac-only limitation. If you're on Windows, wait another 6–12 months for the beta to mature.

#9729. Why AI-Native Organizations Don't Always Need Flatter Teams

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

AI changes different organizational boundaries in different ways.

AI-native is often treated as shorthand for flatter teams, fewer people, and fewer boundaries. That confuses what AI can do with what an organization should become.

I do not think companies are moving toward one final “AI-native” organizational model.

Some boundaries exist because people cannot carry enough knowledge or context. Others separate competing priorities, limit authority, assign accountability, preserve independent checks, or reflect regulatory and physical constraints.

Some of those boundaries will disappear. Others are still there for a reason, even if AI makes them easier to cross.

Before flattening teams, removing handoffs, or giving agents more authority, ask what problem the boundary was solving—and whether AI has actually removed that problem.

No one can become a great salesperson, accountant, lawyer, security engineer, and supply-chain planner at the same time. Attention, memory, training time, and available context are limited, so companies divide knowledge across roles. People usually deal with familiar problems themselves and call in specialists when they need deeper expertise.

AI changes this constraint. An agent can look across far more information than any one person could keep track of, connect context from different parts of the business, and work with tools that used to belong to separate teams.

Take a strategic customer asking for a rush order.

All four can see the same facts and still disagree, because they are responsible for different things.

The company still has to choose what it is willing to sacrifice: margin for growth, stability for a key customer, or risk for speed. AI can make the trade-off clearer. It cannot make the trade-off go away.

Most companies would hesitate to let one person propose a transaction, approve it, execute it, and then review their own work. Separating those steps helps prevent fraud and hidden mistakes. This is the basic logic behind segregation of duties.

With AI agents, this separation becomes easier to blur. One agent may be technically able to propose, approve, execute, and review the same action. Capability is not authority.

Handoffs to specialists add waiting and force people to pass context back and forth.

AI can remove a lot of that friction. But that does not mean every boundary should disappear.

A customer-service employee used to ask the Order team, wait for a response, contact Finance, explain the context again, and wait again.

An agent can now check the customer, order, payment, and policy, then trigger a refund, update the record, and create a ticket in one flow. What used to require several people and systems can now happen in one flow.

But doing more does not give the agent the right to decide more. It can act across systems while still being constrained by policies, limits, and approval rules.

That is where the organizational problem starts. An agent may be able to trigger a refund even though the team running it does not own the refund policy or the payment process.

The real test is what happens when the agent cannot decide. If it can work across five teams but no one owns the exception, the process simply stops.

AI is strongest when the company already knows what it wants to do: establish the facts, apply the rules, execute the policy.

If the order system says an item shipped while the billing system says it was never paid for, the job is mostly to establish what happened. If customers order 100 units but only 80 are available, software can handle much of the allocation once the company has already decided who gets priority and how low margins can go.

The hard part begins when the business has not agreed on the rule.

AI can compare the options, but it cannot decide what the business is willing to sacrifice.

Some of those choices can be made in advance and built into the workflow.

But some decisions do not fit a simple rule. A long-term customer asking for an exception may force a real judgment between margin and the relationship.

AI also forces companies to make explicit choices that used to stay buried inside meetings, manager judgment, and exception handling. It can make coordination cheaper. It does not make disagreement disappear.

Agents can plan and adapt, but only inside a goal, limits, and authority someone else has set.

“Make the company better” is not enough. Better could mean revenue, margin, market share, customer satisfaction, or lower risk. AI can optimize against a set of priorities. Choosing those priorities is not an optimization problem. It is a business judgment.

One of the biggest mistakes in AI-native design is treating process, decision rights, and organizational structure as if they move together. They do not. In practice, at least three different things can change:

When these layers move at different speeds, predictable problems appear:

Change one layer without the others, and you often move the bottleneck instead of removing it.

Do not start from the org chart. Start from the capability the business needs and the outcome it must deliver.

Redesign the work first. Change the organization only where the work actually demands it.

If a handoff exists mainly because people cannot access the same information, carry enough context, or cover a wide enough scope, AI may remove much of the reason for it. That can justify broader roles, less coordination, more end-to-end ownership, and in some cases flatter teams.

But not every boundary should disappear. AI can make Sales and Finance easier to coordinate. It does not give them the same objective. Sales still cares about growth. Finance still cares about margin.

Sometimes redesigning the workflow is not enough. Even if people and agents can handle new-customer setup almost end to end, the work may still stall because ownership is fragmented across teams. Then the organization itself has to change.

This is the logic behind the Reverse Conway Maneuver: sometimes the team structure has to change because the work has changed—not because “AI-native” demands a flatter org chart.

An agent can become very good at operating inside a system. The harder question is who gets to rewrite the system.

Processing a refund under the current policy is execution. Changing the policy, expanding the agent's authority, or redefining how success is measured changes the system the agent operates inside.

Execution should inform those changes. It should not control them.

The same agent should not be able to do the work, judge its own performance, redefine success, and expand its own authority.

As agents take over more execution, people shift toward setting goals, changing rules, handling exceptions, and owning the consequences.

Once the outcome is clear, ask what each boundary is still doing.

AI is not magic, and “AI-native” is not a mandate to redesign everything.

Some organizations should change dramatically. Others may adopt AI deeply while keeping much of the same structure.

A boundary can be inefficient and still be doing important work. Before removing it, understand what you might lose with it.

AI Agents and Legacy Systems: When to Modernize and When to Wait

#9722. The Real Problem With Memecoins Is the Way They’re Traded

Building and learning in the fintech space.

Building and learning in the fintech space.

Building and learning in the fintech space.

Memecoins don't need to be banned, tamed or ignored but simply need a new trading structure or vehicle, one that does not feel flimsy, to say the least. In this regard, vaults have become a tool that can give this asset class a future beyond their current casino like existence.

Proof that the category is growing came in September, when a trader turned $2,972 into just over $2.1 million in under 12 hours, although most of it is still held as the MEME token and subject to volatility. The MEME token, an asset on the controversial Robinhood Chain that rallied more than 3,100x in a day, was born as a jab at AMC chief executive Adam Aron, who had called Robinhood's tokenized AMC shares "contemptible."

From the outside looking in, the entire episode looked absurd, but at the end of the day it took place on rails built by a publicly listed US broker, and that detail in itself is hard to ignore.

It is no secret that, so far, most professional money entering digital assets has moved through crypto ETFs (particularly Bitcoin-related ones). CoinMarketCap's head of research, Alice Liu, summed up this trend, noting:

"Institutions are buying Bitcoin through ETFs. Retail is trading everything else through a phone."

And while such regulated doorways into memecoins also exist, they have barely been used. For instance, US Dogecoin ETFs spent August logging inflows of just hundreds of thousands of dollars as opposed to the billions flowing into Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and XRP.

In fairness, the caution isn't misplaced given that major meme tokens routinely fall double digits in value over the course of a few days. Plus, there is also the threat of manipulation, with CertiK tallying $488 million in September losses alone ($387 million of which was tied to exploits) in relation to crypto assets.

Lastly, retail isn't only trading memecoins onchain, but trading stocks there too, as tokenized equities topped 4 billion in assets on chain in September. To put it quite simply, the line between "crypto" and "traditional" assets is fading on the same venues, in the same wallets, and often in the same liquidity pools.

Amidst all of this, crypto vaults have come in and put forth a unique proposition, acting as smart contract wrappers around a defined strategy such that what goes in, how they're weighted, where the yield comes from, and when capital can be withdrawn are all set out upfront. The model is already being used to bring private credit, tokenized equities and commodities onchain, and there is no obvious reason it can't carry riskier assets as well. In practice, that could take a few forms, such as:

Position limits, audits and redemption terms can be written into the product itself rather than left to a trader's discipline, though each one does a different job.

For instance, position limits cap how much of the vault can sit in any single asset, so with rebalancing a memecoin sleeve set at, say, 5% stays at 5% whether the token doubles or crashes.  An audit, in this regard, checks the smart contract code for bugs and known attack paths. It lowers the odds of an exploit but doesn't guarantee one won't happen, and it says nothing about whether the assets inside are a good bet.

Redemption terms set out how and when depositors can take money out, and they only mean something if they match how easily the underlying assets can actually be sold. A vault that promises instant withdrawals while holding thinly traded memecoins is making a promise the market may not let it keep. The USP (of such a framework) is such that some of the biggest names in finance have also arrived at the same conclusion.

Most recently, Ondo Finance launched Ondo Intelligent Portfolios, a product line that packages BlackRock-designed model strategies into single transferable tokens. The first three (BLKHIon, BLKDIGon and BLKGRWon) target high income, diversified growth and high growth, with constituents, weights and every rebalance visible onchain and rebalancing handled at the smart contract level.

DeFi-native builders too have approached the same idea but with a twist. Valdora, for instance, runs vaults and liquid staking on ZIGChain, curated by risk profile across private credit, quant strategies and tokenized equities. The firm’s setup illustrates what investors should expect from any vault, i.e. how each strategy works, where its yield comes from and what the risks are (all laid out before a deposit is made, with the underlying infrastructure going through independent security audits).

None of this, however, means that pension funds need to start buying dog-themed tokens but it does entail the start of a new, more mature conversation. Memecoins are, among other things, a real-time read on retail risk appetite. On Sept. 10, for example, the sector traded roughly 12% of its $28.8 billion market cap in a single day. That's one snapshot rather than a daily norm, and heavy trading alone doesn't make a market fit for institutions, but it does show how much retail money is moving through the space.

Furthermore, given that tokenized stocks are already doing billions on Uniswap (with tokenized gold trading at a pace that dwarfed last year's metrics easily), the pieces seem to already be onchain and in motion. In all of this, what's still missing is a structure sturdy enough to hold them responsibly, and a vault only fits that bill if it gets a few things right.

For starters, it has to cap memecoin exposure at a size the rest of the portfolio can absorb, publish its holdings and rebalances onchain, set withdrawal terms that match how quickly its assets can really be sold, and spell out the risks in plain language before anyone deposits. Audited code is part of that, not the whole of it. Even a vault that ticks every box won't make memecoins safe, but it can make the risk visible, sized and honest, which is more than the current casino setup offers.

Building and learning in the fintech space.

#9721. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

#9714. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9708. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.
